normal-and-abnormal-labor.scope: Latent vs active first stage, second stage, active phase protraction and arrest (oxytocin, cesarean), false labor (Braxton Hicks), operative vaginal delivery, labor induction
normal-and-abnormal-labor.core: True labor produces progressive cervical change; dystocia management depends on stage, contraction adequacy, fetal status, and descent.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Nulliparity, obesity, fetal macrosomia, malposition, cephalopelvic disproportion, inadequate uterine contractions

rows.label: Clues
items: Assess membrane status, presentation, fetal heart tracing, serial dilation, station, and maternal vital signs
★ Tachysystole: **>5 contractions/10 minutes**, averaged over 30 minutes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysfunctional powers, passenger, or passage → delayed dilation or descent

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Active arrest requires ruptured membranes: no change after **4 hours adequate** or 6 hours inadequate contractions
Adequate: ≥200 Montevideo units (summed mm Hg/10 minutes); IUPC when external assessment insufficient
Prolonged pushing: >3 hours nulliparous, >2 hours multiparous; individualize by descent and fetal status
Failed induction requires ≥12–18 hours oxytocin after ROM; slow latent phase alone does not mandate cesarean
Presenting part unpalpable → **ultrasound** for lie/presentation before amniotomy; floating part → cord prolapse risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Protraction (<1 cm/2 hours) with weak contractions → **oxytocin**, amniotomy; established active arrest → cesarean
Tachysystole → stop oxytocin, lateral positioning; persistent fetal compromise → terbutaline, expedited delivery
★ Operative birth: full dilation, ruptured membranes, engaged head, known position, skilled operator; failed → cesarean
Unfavorable cervix → balloon or prostaglandin ripening, then oxytocin; avoid misoprostol after prior cesarean
Labor pain → **epidural** most effective first-stage; pudendal block covers second stage only

rows.label: Complications
items: Maternal infection, hemorrhage, exhaustion; neonatal hypoxia
Forceps/vacuum → lacerations, scalp injury; vacuum → subgaleal hemorrhage, avoid <34 weeks or face presentation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Induce for maternal/fetal indications or offer elective induction from 39 weeks; no elective earlier delivery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Braxton Hicks: irregular, self-resolving, no cervical change → reassurance; GBS prophylaxis only in true labor/rupture
Obstructed labor: strong contractions, no progress; CPD (macrosomia), achondroplastic pelvis, transverse lie → **cesarean**, not oxytocin
Shoulder dystocia: head delivered, shoulders impacted; failed head descent at full dilation → CPD

table.title: Stages
rows: 6–10 cm; older exams may use ≥5 cm

osteoporosis.name: Osteoporosis
osteoporosis.scope: DEXA scan T-score criteria, screening guidelines, glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, vertebral compression fractures, bisphosphonates
osteoporosis.core: Fragility fracture or markedly reduced bone density identifies skeletal weakness, often silent until hip or vertebral fracture.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Postmenopause, older age, White/Asian ancestry, BMI <20, parental fragility hip fracture, smoking, alcohol >2 drinks/day
Glucocorticoids, early or surgical menopause, hypogonadism, malabsorption, hyperthyroidism, immobility, rheumatoid arthritis

rows.label: Clues
items: Height loss, kyphosis, acute back pain with **midline point tenderness** after trivial strain suggest vertebral compression
Neurologic deficits, fever, or nocturnal pain suggest alternative spinal pathology

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Bone resorption exceeds formation; microarchitecture deteriorates despite normally mineralized remaining bone
Estrogen deficiency increases osteoclast activity; steroids suppress osteoblasts and reduce calcium balance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Hip/spine DXA**; use T-scores in postmenopausal women and men ≥50
★ Hip/vertebral low-trauma fracture establishes diagnosis regardless of DXA; acute vertebral pain → **spine x-ray** before DXA
CBC, calcium, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, 25-OH vitamin D; targeted secondary-cause testing
Younger adults: Z-score ≤−2 suggests below-age bone density; T-score alone insufficient

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Alendronate or zoledronic acid** for qualifying fracture, osteoporosis-range DXA, or high FRAX risk; raloxifene/estrogen contraindicated after VTE
Osteopenia: treat if 10-year hip risk ≥3% or major osteoporotic risk ≥20%
Oral bisphosphonate: fasting water, remain upright; avoid esophageal disease, hypocalcemia, severe kidney dysfunction
Very high risk → teriparatide/romosozumab then antiresorptive; stopping denosumab requires follow-on antiresorptive
Vertebral pain: analgesia, mobilization, short bracing; procedures reserved for selected refractory cases

rows.label: Complications
items: ★ **Hip fracture** → immobility, thromboembolism, excess mortality
Bisphosphonates: rare jaw osteonecrosis/atypical femur fracture; denosumab: hypocalcemia, rebound vertebral fractures

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Screen **women ≥65**, younger postmenopausal women at increased risk; evidence insufficient for routine male screening
**Smoking cessation**, less heavy alcohol outrank supplements; weight-bearing/resistance exercise, fall prevention, dietary calcium/vitamin D
Prednisone-equivalent ≥2.5 mg/day for >3 months → fracture-risk assessment; prevent with **alendronate**, not estrogen/raloxifene

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomalacia: defective mineralization, low phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase
Myeloma: anemia, renal injury, lytic lesions; metastatic fracture: destructive focal lesion

osteoporosis.evidence: Screening checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF 2025](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/osteoporosis-screening%20); treatment: established fracture-risk framework.

ovarian-cancer.name: Ovarian cancer
ovarian-cancer.scope: Epithelial ovarian carcinoma, CA-125, pelvic ultrasound, peritoneal carcinomatosis, germ cell tumors, sex cord-stromal tumors, surgical staging and cytoreduction, platinum-based chemotherapy
ovarian-cancer.core: Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic symptoms, or an adnexal mass—especially after menopause—requires evaluation for an often late-presenting malignancy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Increasing age, nulliparity, BRCA1/2 or Lynch syndrome; family history of breast/ovarian cancer
Endometriosis associated with clear-cell/endometrioid subtypes; pregnancy and combined contraceptives reduce epithelial risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Older patient + ascites, large/fixed pelvic mass, weight loss, pleural effusion, obstruction → **epithelial** carcinoma
Young patient with rapidly enlarging mass → germ cell tumor; estrogen/androgen effects → stromal tumor
Postmenopausal bleeding with adnexal mass → consider estrogen-secreting granulosa tumor and endometrial disease
★ **Palpable ovary after menopause** → abnormal (ovaries atrophy); pelvic ultrasound

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Many high-grade serous tumors arise in distal fallopian tube epithelium
Transcoelomic seeding produces peritoneal/omental disease; hormone secretion depends on tumor lineage

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Transvaginal ultrasound** first; solid components, papillary projections, vascularity, ascites increase suspicion
★ **CA-125** supports risk assessment/monitoring, not diagnosis or average-risk screening
Young/complex mass → β-hCG, AFP, LDH; suspected stromal tumor → inhibin/sex hormones
Suspected malignancy → CT abdomen/pelvis/chest and gynecologic oncology; definitive histology and staging usually surgical
Isolated resectable mass → avoid aspiration; advanced disease → biopsy before neoadjuvant chemotherapy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Epithelial carcinoma → **surgical staging/cytoreduction + carboplatin/paclitaxel** according to stage
Poor upfront surgical candidate → tissue confirmation, neoadjuvant platinum chemotherapy, interval cytoreduction
Germ cell malignancy → fertility-sparing surgery when feasible; stage IA dysgerminoma may avoid chemotherapy
Higher-risk germ cell tumors → bleomycin/etoposide/cisplatin
Selected BRCA/HRD-associated disease → PARP-inhibitor maintenance after platinum response

rows.label: Complications
items: Peritoneal carcinomatosis, ascites, malignant obstruction, VTE; chemotherapy neuropathy/myelosuppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **No routine CA-125/ultrasound screening** in asymptomatic average-risk patients
Genetic counseling/testing; hereditary high-risk patients → discuss risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing

rows.label: Mimics
items: Endometrioma: cyclic pain, ground-glass ultrasound; CA-125 can rise
Meigs syndrome: benign ovarian fibroma plus ascites/pleural effusion; no peritoneal implants

table.title: Tumor markers
rows: Often bilateral; psammoma bodies; WT1+, p53 abnormal

polycystic-ovary-syndrome.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.scope: Rotterdam criteria (hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, polycystic ovaries), metabolic risks, weight loss, oral contraceptives, ovulation induction (letrozole, clomiphene)
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.core: Hyperandrogenism and chronic ovulatory dysfunction after exclusion of alternative causes suggest PCOS; management follows metabolic, menstrual and fertility priorities.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, insulin resistance and obesity; lean patients can also have PCOS
Pubertal transition can mimic disease, requiring stricter adolescent diagnostic criteria

rows.label: Clues
items: Irregular/infrequent menses, episodic heavy bleeding, infertility, hirsutism, acne or androgenic alopecia
Acanthosis nigricans suggests hyperinsulinemia; obesity is supportive, not required
Rapid virilization, deep voice or markedly elevated androgens → investigate tumor rather than assume PCOS

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insulin resistance and ovarian androgen excess impair follicular maturation and ovulation
Absent cyclic progesterone permits persistent estrogen-driven endometrial proliferation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Adults: **2 of 3 Rotterdam** features—hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, polycystic ovarian morphology
Exclude mimics: **hCG, TSH, prolactin, morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone**; latter screens nonclassic CAH
Total/free testosterone; **clinical hirsutism/acne** suffices despite normal levels; DHEAS if adrenal source suspected
★ Irregular cycles plus hyperandrogenism → **ultrasound not required**; LH:FSH ratio not diagnostic
BP, lipid profile and **oral glucose tolerance test** assess metabolic risk; adolescent diagnosis avoids ultrasound criteria

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Lifestyle/weight management first for all; modest weight loss can restore ovulation in overweight patients
★ No pregnancy desired → **combined OCP** for cycles/androgen symptoms; cyclic progestin or LNG-IUD protects endometrium
Persistent hirsutism → spironolactone with reliable contraception; allow months for hair response
Metabolic risk/insulin resistance → metformin; less effective than OCP for androgen symptoms
★ Anovulatory infertility → **letrozole first-line**; clomiphene alternative, older exams may expect it; check other factors

rows.label: Complications
items: Endometrial hyperplasia/cancer, infertility, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, OSA and depression
Pregnancy → increased gestational diabetes and hypertensive-disorder risk
Gonadotropin ovulation induction → high multiple-gestation risk, so letrozole/clomiphene first

rows.label: Prevention
items: Regular progestin exposure for prolonged amenorrhea; persistent abnormal bleeding → endometrial assessment
Periodic glycemic/BP/lipid reassessment; preconception metabolic optimization and folate

rows.label: Mimics
items: Androgen-secreting tumor: rapid progression, severe virilization
Nonclassic CAH: elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone
Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea: low estrogen with exercise/energy deficit

preterm-labor.name: Preterm labor
preterm-labor.scope: Preterm labor (<37 weeks), cervical insufficiency, tocolysis (indomethacin, nifedipine), antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone), magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection, GBS chemoprophylaxis
preterm-labor.core: Regular contractions with cervical change before 37 weeks; briefly delay eligible early births to improve neonatal outcomes, without prolonging unsafe pregnancies.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior spontaneous preterm birth, short cervix, multiple gestation, infection, smoking, uterine anomalies
Cervical surgery or prior painless second-trimester loss suggests cervical insufficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Pelvic pressure, backache, increased discharge, contractions; assess membrane rupture and bleeding
Fever, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia → intraamniotic infection; maternal/fetal instability changes delivery timing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Premature inflammatory/uterine activation versus mechanically weak cervix with painless dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Sterile speculum examination** for pooling and cervix; ultrasound dates pregnancy and assesses presentation
Transvaginal cervical length; selected symptomatic cases: negative fetal fibronectin predicts low imminent birth risk
Collect GBS culture, urine studies; exclude previa before digital examination with bleeding

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Birth within 7 days, **24–33 6/7 weeks** → betamethasone; selected untreated 34–36 6/7-week pregnancies also eligible
★ Delivery expected <32 weeks → **magnesium sulfate** for neuroprotection, not primary tocolysis
Tocolysis: 48 hours for steroids/transfer; no maintenance; late-preterm steroids avoided with pregestational diabetes
★ **No tocolysis** with infection, significant abruption, severe preeclampsia, or fetal compromise; proceed toward delivery
Intrapartum penicillin for positive/unknown GBS; no routine antibiotics for intact membranes without infection

rows.label: Complications
items: Neonatal RDS, IVH, NEC, sepsis, cerebral palsy; magnesium toxicity → hyporeflexia, respiratory depression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Singleton short cervix ≤20 mm before 24 weeks → vaginal progesterone; consider at 21–25 mm
Cervical insufficiency/prior qualifying loss → cerclage; prior preterm birth + cervix <25 mm before 24 weeks
17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate withdrawn 2023; progesterone without short cervix not routinely recommended
Older exam questions may expect 17-hydroxyprogesterone from 16–20 weeks after prior spontaneous preterm birth

rows.label: Mimics
items: Braxton Hicks: no progressive dilation
Cervical insufficiency: painless dilation, minimal contractions
PPROM: membrane rupture precedes labor; distinct latency-antibiotic pathway

pubertal-development.name: Pubertal development
pubertal-development.scope: Tanner stages, normal thelarche vs breast mass, premature adrenarche, precocious puberty, constitutional delay of growth and puberty
pubertal-development.core: Interpret sexual maturation by sequence, age, growth velocity, and bone age; isolated benign variants lack progressive gonadal activation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Constitutional delay often familial; chronic illness, undernutrition, excess exercise delay maturation
CNS lesions, gonadal/adrenal hormone excess, exogenous sex steroids can cause early puberty

rows.label: Clues
items: Girls: breast budding precedes peak growth, then menarche about 2–3 years later
Boys: testes enlarge before penile growth; pubic hair reflects adrenarche, not necessarily gonadarche
★ Asymmetric tender **subareolar breast bud** at expected age usually normal; hard eccentric mass needs evaluation
Rapid height acceleration, advancing secondary characteristics, neurologic symptoms → pathologic early maturation concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Central puberty: hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility → LH/FSH → gonadal steroids
Adrenarche produces adrenal androgens independently; peripheral hormone excess suppresses pituitary gonadotropins
Immature hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis → irregular anovulatory cycles, normal for 2–3 years after menarche
Virilized boy with **prepubertal testes** → peripheral androgen, usually adrenal; central puberty enlarges testes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Precocious: secondary sexual development **before 8 years girls or 9 years boys**
★ Delayed: **no breasts by 13**, no testes ≥4 mL by 14; evaluate absent menarche by 15
Growth chart, Tanner examination, bone age; LH/FSH, estradiol/testosterone, TSH selected by pattern
Central precocity → pubertal basal/stimulated LH; brain MRI especially boys, young girls, neurologic signs
Peripheral pattern → targeted adrenal/gonadal tests/imaging; isolated adrenarche requires exclusion of rapid virilization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Progressive central precocity → **GnRH agonist**; treat CNS cause when present
Peripheral precocity → remove hormone source or treat tumor/adrenal disorder; GnRH agonist alone ineffective
Constitutional delay → reassurance, follow growth; distress → specialist-guided brief sex-steroid course
Benign premature thelarche/adrenarche → observe progression; no automatic hormonal treatment
Pubertal gynecomastia, unilateral or bilateral, smooth subareolar → **reassurance**; no labs/biopsy; carcinoma very rare

rows.label: Complications
items: Early epiphyseal closure → reduced adult height; psychosocial distress
Missed hypogonadism → impaired bone accrual; untreated CNS/tumor cause may progress

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate nutrition, manage chronic disease, avoid household hormone exposure; serial growth surveillance
Normal puberty + moodiness, mild parent conflict → **puberty education** for child, parents; no drug testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: Primary gonadal failure: high LH/FSH, low sex steroids
Permanent central hypogonadism: absent progression rather than eventual familial catch-up
Familial short stature: short parents, bone age matches chronologic age; constitutional delay: **delayed bone age**

table.title: Tanner staging anchors
rows: Further enlargement; menarche usually within 1–2 years

pubertal-development.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric endocrine timing and Tanner staging.

rh-alloimmunization.name: Rh alloimmunization
rh-alloimmunization.scope: Rh(D) and other red cell alloimmunization (Kell, Duffy), anti-D immune globulin prophylaxis, indirect Coombs titer monitoring, fetomaternal hemorrhage (Kleihauer-Betke), middle cerebral artery Doppler for fetal anemia
rh-alloimmunization.core: Maternal IgG against fetal red-cell antigens crosses the placenta, causing fetal anemia, hydrops, and neonatal hemolysis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Antigen-negative mother/positive fetus; prior pregnancy, transfusion, bleeding, trauma, invasive procedures
Anti-D, anti-Kell, and anti-Duffy clinically significant; ABO incompatibility usually milder

rows.label: Clues
items: Often asymptomatic mother; fetal ascites, skin edema, placentomegaly, cardiomegaly
Neonate: early jaundice, pallor, reticulocytosis, **positive direct Coombs**; severe disease → cardiovascular collapse

rows.label: Pathophys
items: First exposure sensitizes; subsequent antigen exposure produces an anamnestic response
Kell antibodies additionally suppress erythropoiesis; low titers can still cause severe disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ First prenatal visit: ABO/Rh type + **indirect Coombs**; repeat before routine antenatal prophylaxis
Antibody → **paternal antigen typing**; negative (certain paternity) → no fetal risk; else fetal typing, titers
★ Critical titer, often **1:16**, or previously affected pregnancy → middle cerebral artery Doppler
MCA peak systolic velocity >1.5 MoM → fetal blood sampling; Kell warrants specialist surveillance
Kleihauer-Betke quantifies hemorrhage for dosing: **300 µg covers 30 mL fetal whole blood**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe preterm fetal anemia → **intrauterine transfusion**; near term → delivery
Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia → phototherapy; severe hemolysis → exchange transfusion

rows.label: Complications
items: High-output heart failure, stillbirth, bilirubin encephalopathy, delayed neonatal anemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Unsensitized Rh-negative mother: **anti-D immune globulin** at 28 weeks and within 72 hours postpartum
Sensitizing event → dose now; lasts ~12 weeks, repeat at 28; postpartum only if Rh-positive/unknown infant
★ Established anti-D sensitization → prophylaxis ineffective; no equivalent prophylaxis for Kell/Duffy
ACOG 2024: routine Rh testing/prophylaxis may be forgone for abortion/loss before 12 weeks

rows.label: Mimics
items: Parvovirus: nonimmune hydrops with negative maternal antibody screen
ABO hemolysis: may affect first pregnancy; fetal hydrops uncommon

rh-alloimmunization.evidence: Prophylaxis checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG Rh guidance](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/the-rh-factor-how-it-can-affect-your-pregnancy), [2024 update](https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000005733); remaining content established teaching.

shoulder-dystocia.name: Shoulder dystocia
shoulder-dystocia.scope: Risk factors (fetal macrosomia, maternal diabetes), obstetric maneuvers (McRoberts, suprapubic pressure), fetal complications (clavicle fracture, Erb palsy C5-C6, Klumpke palsy C8-T1), maternal lacerations
shoulder-dystocia.core: After fetal head delivery, failure of shoulders to emerge with gentle traction is an obstetric emergency requiring maneuvers to release impaction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Macrosomia, maternal diabetes/obesity, prior shoulder dystocia, prolonged second stage, operative vaginal delivery
Many cases occur without identifiable risks; fetal weight estimation predicts imperfectly

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Turtle sign**: delivered head retracts against perineum; external rotation/shoulder delivery fails
Call immediately rather than repeatedly pulling on the fetal head

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Anterior shoulder usually trapped behind pubic symphysis; less commonly posterior shoulder against sacral promontory
Cord compression and impaired thoracic expansion rapidly threaten oxygenation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis after head delivery**; no imaging or laboratory confirmation
Note head-delivery time, summon obstetric/anesthesia/neonatal team, identify fetal orientation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First: **McRoberts maneuver + suprapubic pressure**; stop maternal pushing temporarily
★ **No fundal pressure or excessive head traction**; both worsen impaction/injury
If unresolved → deliver posterior arm, internal rotational Rubin/Woods maneuvers, or hands-and-knees positioning
Episiotomy only creates access for internal maneuvers; does not relieve bony impaction
Refractory: expert cephalic replacement (Zavanelli) followed by cesarean; other rescue maneuvers individualized

rows.label: Complications
items: Fetal hypoxic injury/death, clavicle/humerus fracture, brachial plexus injury
Maternal postpartum hemorrhage, third/fourth-degree perineal tears; inspect injuries after delivery

rows.label: Prevention
items: Consider cesarean for EFW ≥5,000 g without diabetes; **≥4,500 g with diabetes**
Optimize glucose; prior event → recurrence counseling; structured team drills improve response
No maneuver reliably predicts/prevents every event; document sequence and neonatal examination

rows.label: Mimics
items: Tight nuchal cord: visible encircling cord rather than fixed shoulder impaction
Breech head entrapment: body delivered first; requires different rescue maneuvers

table.title: Neonatal plexus findings
rows: Adducted internally rotated arm, extended elbow; grasp preserved

skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.name: Skin and soft tissue infections
skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.scope: Cellulitis, erysipelas, folliculitis, furuncles, carbuncles, lymphangitis, necrotizing fasciitis
skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.core: Skin infection management depends on purulence, systemic illness, and signs of deep tissue destruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Skin breaks, tinea pedis, edema/lymphedema, diabetes, obesity, injection drug use
Prior MRSA, crowding, recent hospitalization; surgery or penetrating trauma raises deep-infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Warmth, tenderness, erythema; rapidly expanding margins or systemic toxicity require urgent reassessment
★ **Pain out of proportion**, bullae, anesthesia, crepitus, shock → necrotizing infection
Perineal infection, especially diabetes → Fournier gangrene/necrotizing fasciitis; saltwater exposure → Vibrio, freshwater → Aeromonas

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nonpurulent infection usually streptococcal, S aureus possible; purulent lesions usually S aureus
Fascial spread, toxins → necrosis, sepsis; minor trauma, no crepitus → **GAS**; crepitus → Clostridium/polymicrobial
Tinea pedis = portal of entry: acute fever/cellulitis is bacterial (S aureus/streptococcal) superinfection, not Trichophyton

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical diagnosis; **bedside ultrasound** if occult fluid collection suspected
Culture drained pus for severe, recurrent, or resistant infection; blood cultures for systemic toxicity
Suspected necrotizing disease → immediate surgical evaluation; imaging must not delay exploration
Low laboratory risk score or absent gas does not exclude necrotizing fasciitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Deep infection → **urgent debridement + vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam**, add clindamycin for toxin suppression
Confirmed group A streptococcal necrotizing infection → penicillin + clindamycin
Moderate cellulitis (systemic signs) → IV cefazolin; MRSA risk or cephalexin failure → vancomycin; severe → + pip-tazo
★ Abscess: add **antibiotics** for systemic signs, immunocompromise, extensive disease, or failed drainage
Pregnancy + suspected MRSA → clindamycin or vancomycin; **no doxycycline or fluoroquinolones**

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacteremia, osteomyelitis, septic thrombophlebitis; tissue loss and amputation
Toxic shock, multiorgan failure; recurrent cellulitis worsens lymphatic dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat interdigital fungal infection, manage edema, skin hygiene, protect wounds
Recurrent staphylococcal infections → consider nasal mupirocin + chlorhexidine decolonization; avoid shared razors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Stasis dermatitis: chronic, often bilateral, itchy
DVT: deep swelling without superficial spreading infection; contact dermatitis: pruritic exposure-pattern rash
Superficial thrombophlebitis: palpable indurated venous cord, not lymphatic streaks

table.title: Superficial patterns
rows: Incision and drainage; TMP-SMX if needed
Tender red streaks from skin break toward nodes
Usually S pyogenes; cephalexin; IV if systemic
Itchy follicular pustules on trunk/thighs after hot tub

skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.evidence: Not checked online; established IDSA-based infection management.

urinary-incontinence.name: Urinary incontinence
urinary-incontinence.core: Involuntary urine leakage is classified by triggers, urgency, bladder emptying, and ability to reach a toilet; reversible contributors often coexist.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Childbirth, pelvic surgery, aging, obesity; diabetes, neurologic disease, prostate enlargement
Diuretics, sedatives, anticholinergics, constipation, infection, impaired mobility/cognition worsen control

rows.label: Clues
items: History: timing, volume, dysuria, weak stream, nocturia, fluid intake, obstetric/surgical and neurologic history
★ **New saddle anesthesia, leg weakness, retention** → urgent cauda equina evaluation
Continuous leakage after pelvic surgery/radiation suggests fistula; recurrent UTIs/hematuria require further investigation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Stress: aging/multiparity weaken pelvic floor → **urethral hypermobility**, low sphincter tone
Urge: **uninhibited detrusor contractions** (detrusor instability), worsened by caffeine; MS lesion → low residual
Overflow: **detrusor underactivity/acontractile bladder** (MS, diabetes, stroke) or outlet obstruction → high residual
Functional impairment can prevent continence despite intact lower urinary tract function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis + voiding diary**, focused pelvic/prostate and neurologic examination; review medications
Cough stress test with reasonably full bladder; assess prolapse, atrophy, fecal impaction
**Q-tip excursion >30°** on Valsalva → urethral hypermobility (urethrocele)
★ Suspected retention/emptying symptoms → **postvoid residual**; persistent >200 mL suggests inadequate emptying
No routine initial urodynamics/cystoscopy; uncertainty, hematuria, refractory symptoms → additional testing

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat reversible contributor; mixed incontinence → target most bothersome component
★ **Pelvic floor training/bladder training** underpin conservative care; weight loss, reduce caffeine, timed voiding
Urgency drugs: mirabegron or antimuscarinic (oxybutynin); discuss cognitive risk and avoid antimuscarinics with retention
Mirabegron may increase BP; avoid severe uncontrolled hypertension; refractory urgency → botulinum toxin or neuromodulation
Genitourinary syndrome of menopause → local vaginal estrogen when suitable; not systemic estrogen for leakage

rows.label: Complications
items: Dermatitis, falls from rushing, social isolation, sleep disruption
Overflow → hydronephrosis/renal injury; bladder botulinum toxin → retention, UTI

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication review, accessible toilet, mobility aids; bowel regularity, maintain strength and weight

rows.label: Mimics
items: Polyuria: high urine volume from hyperglycemia/diuresis rather than primary storage failure
Vaginal fistula: constant leakage unrelated to voiding urge or exertion

urinary-tract-infections.name: Urinary tract infections
urinary-tract-infections.scope: Asymptomatic bacteriuria, acute cystitis, pyelonephritis, catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI), catheter removal, empiric antibiotics
urinary-tract-infections.core: Symptoms localize urinary infection: bladder disease lacks systemic illness; renal involvement causes fever or flank pain; bacteriuria alone is insufficient.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual activity, spermicides, pregnancy, obstruction/stones, urinary retention, instrumentation
Catheter duration, diabetes, prior resistant isolates or antibiotics increase complicated-course risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort; absent vaginal discharge supports urinary source
★ **Rigors, CVA tenderness, vomiting, hypotension** → pyelonephritis or urosepsis
Catheterized patients: new urinary/systemic symptoms; cloudy urine or pyuria alone insufficient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Usually ascending enteric bacteria, predominantly E coli; catheter biofilm maintains colonization
Urease-producing Proteus alkalinizes urine → struvite calculi and persistent infection
Pregnancy: progesterone ureteral relaxation + uterine compression → **stasis**; physiologic right-sided ureteral dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis**: pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites; pyelonephritis → heavy pyuria, WBC clumps/casts; negative nitrites don't exclude
Culture: pyelonephritis, pregnancy, CAUTI, recurrence/resistance; classic cystitis often clinical
Persistent fever after 48–72 hours, sepsis, or suspected obstruction → renal imaging
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: usually ≥100,000 CFU/mL; delirium alone → seek other causes without automatic antibiotics
Febrile non-toilet-trained child → **catheterized** urinalysis/culture; bag/clean-catch contaminate

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria only in pregnancy or before urologic mucosal trauma** in routine adult scenarios
★ CAUTI → **remove unnecessary catheter**; if needed and present >2 weeks, replace before culture/treatment
★ Infected obstructed collecting system → **urgent drainage + IV antibiotics**; antibiotics alone insufficient
Improving nonpregnant pyelonephritis: fluoroquinolone 5–7 days, other active drugs 7 days; high-risk cases individualized
Febrile infant → **cefotaxime/ceftriaxone**; first-generation cefazolin inadequate

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacteremia, septic shock, renal/perinephric abscess; pregnancy → preterm birth
Antibiotics → resistance, C difficile; fluoroquinolones → tendon injury, QT prolongation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid unnecessary catheters; closed drainage, daily removal assessment
Postmenopausal recurrence → vaginal estrogen
Recurrence ≥3/year or ≥2 in 6 months → postcoital or daily nitrofurantoin/TMP-SMX
Sporadic postcoital cystitis → **void before/after intercourse**; stop diaphragm/spermicide; condoms don't prevent

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vaginitis: discharge, pruritus, external burning
Urethritis: sexual exposure, discharge, positive gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT
Bladder pain syndrome: chronic symptoms, repeatedly negative cultures

table.title: Initial antibiotics; tailor to culture/resistance
rows: Ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin; initial ceftriaxone if resistance risk
IV fluids + ceftriaxone; cefepime/piperacillin-tazobactam if Pseudomonas risk
Avoid nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin: inadequate renal tissue levels

vaginitis.name: Vaginitis
vaginitis.scope: Bacterial vaginosis, Trichomoniasis, Vulvovaginal candidiasis, atrophic vaginitis, genitourinary syndrome of menopause
vaginitis.core: Vaginal discharge or irritation requires distinction among dysbiosis, sexually transmitted protozoal infection, yeast overgrowth, and hypoestrogenic mucosal change.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: BV: new partners, douching; trichomoniasis: sexual exposure
Candida: antibiotics, pregnancy, diabetes, immunosuppression; atrophy: menopause or other hypoestrogenic states
Prepubertal: hand inoculation of respiratory pathogens during URI

rows.label: Clues
items: Pruritus, dysuria, dyspareunia; discharge appearance overlaps, so symptoms alone insufficient
★ **Fever, lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness** → evaluate PID rather than isolated vaginitis
Postmenopausal bleeding needs assessment beyond assuming atrophy
★ Prepubertal **foul purulent/bloody discharge** → retained vaginal **foreign body**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: BV: lactobacilli depleted, anaerobes expand; Candida causes inflammatory overgrowth
Low estrogen thins epithelium and reduces lactobacilli → mucosal fragility and elevated vaginal pH

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Vaginal pH, saline/KOH microscopy**, history and examination; NAAT improves infectious diagnosis
BV: ≥3 Amsel—discharge, ↑pH, clue cells, amine odor; Gardnerella culture unhelpful (normal flora)
★ Suspected trichomoniasis + negative wet mount → **NAAT**, not reassurance
Recurrent/complicated Candida → culture or PCR for species; asymptomatic colonization alone needs no treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Trichomoniasis → **oral metronidazole 7 days in women**; treat partners, abstain until completed/resolved
BV → oral metronidazole 7 days or vaginal metronidazole/clindamycin, **no routine partner treatment**, ACOG: treat if recurrent; treat symptomatic pregnancy
Candida → topical azole/nystatin or oral fluconazole; **pregnancy: topical azole 7 days**, avoid oral fluconazole
GSM → moisturizers/lubricants, then low-dose vaginal estrogen for persistent symptoms
Recurrent BV: ACOG 2025 considers male-partner metronidazole + topical clindamycin; older boards omit

rows.label: Complications
items: BV/trichomoniasis associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes and increased STI acquisition
Recurrent symptoms → reassess diagnosis, adherence, reinfection, diabetes or resistant/non-albicans yeast

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Trichomoniasis → **retest women at about 3 months**; condoms
Avoid douching/irritants; no routine partner treatment for uncomplicated Candida

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cervicitis: endocervical mucopus, friability, positive GC/CT NAAT
Contact dermatitis: external irritation after product exposure
Sarcoma botryoides: girl with bleeding, grape-like polypoid vaginal mass
